\chapter{Two Words Where English Has One}
\label{ch:hi-sambandh}
\hlchaptermodality{101}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say who I am with and without, place a thing in front of, behind or near a landmark, say who something is for, and say what I am doing something in order to do.}

Answer a directions question with a landmark rather than a distance, and say which of the three place words would be the wrong answer to a question about side.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ke sāth]{\hi{के} \hi{साथ} — with, in two words}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-saath}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{his} and \emph{her} in Hindi, and notice that both were the same word wearing different endings. Now try to say \textbf{with my friend}, and notice that English needs exactly one word to do it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{साथ}}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ} \hi{हूँ।}} — I am with a friend.

English spends one word on this. Hindi spends \textbf{two}, and only the second one is new.

\subsection*{The two words}
Take the phrase apart and something familiar falls out:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{what it is} \\
\midrule
\hi{दोस्त} & the noun \\
\hi{के} & \textbf{\hi{उसका}'s ending}, standing on its own \\
\hi{साथ} & the new word — \emph{company} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \textbf{\hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ}} is, piece by piece, \emph{the friend's company}. Hindi is not reaching for a preposition at all. It is building a possessive and then naming the relation as a thing.

That is why the first word is \textbf{\hi{के}} and never \textbf{\hi{का}}: a possessive agrees with what follows it, and \textbf{\hi{साथ}} is masculine and standing in front of a further word, so it takes the oblique ending you met on nouns one chapter ago.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a shape, not a word}]
Write the shape down once, because the rest of this chapter is the same shape six more times:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot} & \textbf{contents} \\
\midrule
1 & the noun \\
2 & \textbf{\hi{के}} \\
3 & the relation word \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{अपने} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ}} — \emph{with my own friend} — puts \textbf{\hi{अपना}} in slot 1's ordinary spot, bent to \textbf{\hi{अपने}} because a postposition is coming. Everything in front of a postposition bends. That has now been true of possessives, of pronouns and of nouns, and it is true here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{अपने} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of the two words is the new one
  \item why the first word is \hi{के} and not \hi{का}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many words does Hindi use for \emph{with}? (Two.) Which one is new? (\textbf{\hi{साथ}}.) What is the other one? (The possessive ending, in its oblique form.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ke binā]{\hi{के} \hi{बिना} — the opposite, for the price of one word}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-binaa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{with a friend} in Hindi. Now say it again and listen to how much of it you would have to change to mean the opposite.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{बिना}}
\textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{बिना}} — without tea.

One word changed. The shape did not move.

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot 3} & \textbf{the whole phrase} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\hi{साथ} & \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ} & with a friend \\
\hi{बिना} & \hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{बिना} & without tea \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

This is what the shape buys. Once slot 3 is a \textbf{swappable position}, every new relation costs exactly one word instead of a new piece of grammar — and this chapter is going to swap it five more times.

English does not work this way. \emph{With} and \emph{without} look related because one is built out of the other, but \emph{in front of} and \emph{behind} are unrelated words that share nothing. In Hindi all of them share \textbf{\hi{के}}, and that is the part that is doing the grammatical work.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two ways to write it}]
\textbf{\hi{बिना}} is the one relation word in this chapter that is also allowed to stand \textbf{in front of} its noun — \textbf{\hi{बिना} \hi{चाय} \hi{के}} is said too, and means the same thing.

Learn the slot-3 version. It is the one that matches everything else you are about to meet, and a reader who knows the ordinary order will still understand the other one when a paper prints it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{बिना}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{बिना}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one slot that changed between \emph{with} and \emph{without}
  \item the word that stayed put in the middle
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{without tea}? (\textbf{\hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{बिना}}.) Which slot carries the meaning? (The third.) Which slot carries the grammar? (The second — \textbf{\hi{के}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ghar ke pās]{\hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास} — the word that was hiding in \emph{I have}}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-paas}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I have} in Hindi. Now look at the two words you said and ask what the second one actually means, because so far you have never been told.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{पास}}
\textbf{\hi{दुकान} \hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास} \hi{है।}} — The shop is near the house.

\textbf{\hi{पास}} means \emph{near}. It has meant \emph{near} the whole time.

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{word for word} & \textbf{the job it does} \\
\midrule
\hi{मेरे} \hi{पास} & near me & I \textbf{have} \\
\hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास} & near the house & it is \textbf{nearby} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The same three slots, and the same slot-3 word. What changed is only what sits in slot 1 — a person or a place.

So Hindi says \emph{having} by saying \textbf{nearness}, and the physical sense you are meeting now is the original one. A language with no verb for \emph{have} reached for the nearest true thing: whatever is beside you is, for practical purposes, yours. The possessive chapter taught you the borrowed meaning first because it is the one a beginner needs first. This is the meaning it was borrowed from.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a place answer}]
You have been able to \textbf{ask} where something is for sixty chapters. This is the first shape that lets you \textbf{answer} with anything more exact than a room:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{question} & \textbf{answer} \\
\midrule
\hi{दुकान} \hi{कहाँ} \hi{है}? & \hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An A1 listening paper does this constantly, because \emph{near} is how people actually give directions — not in metres, but relative to a landmark both speakers already know.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दुकान} \hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \textbf{\hi{पास}} means on its own
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मेरे} \hi{पास}\textquotedblright{} and the job it does
  \item why a language with no verb for \emph{have} might use this word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\hi{पास}} mean? (Near.) Which slot does it occupy? (The third.) Which of its two jobs did you learn first, and which came first in the language? (Having, then nearness — the other way round.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ke sāmne]{\hi{के} \hi{सामने} — in front of}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-saamne}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{near the house}. Now say the word for a railway station. You are one word away from the sentence an A1 listening paper is most likely to set you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{सामने}}
\textbf{\hi{दुकान} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} \hi{है।}} — The shop is in front of the station.

\subsection*{The two words}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
\hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{पास} & near the station \\
\hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} & in front of the station \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English changed from one word to three. Hindi changed from one word to one.

Notice what \textbf{\hi{सामने}} does not do. It ends in \textbf{-\hi{ए}}, which on an adjective would be an ending that agrees with something — but this word never changes, whoever or whatever is in front of whatever. \textbf{A slot-three word is fixed.} The bending in this shape all happens in slot 2, and slot 2 is already done before slot 3 arrives.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: front of what}]
English \emph{in front of} is ambiguous in a way Hindi's is not. \emph{In front of the station} can mean the near side of the building, or it can mean a position further along the road. \textbf{\hi{के} \hi{सामने}} means the first: \textbf{facing it, across from it, on the side you would stand to look at it.}

That is the reading a direction-giver intends, and the reading an exam item expects.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दुकान} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दुकान} \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{पास} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{} — the weaker claim
  \item whether \textbf{\hi{सामने}} ever changes its ending
  \item which slot does all the bending in this shape
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{in front of the station}? (\textbf{\hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने}}.) Does the third word agree with anything? (No — it is fixed.) Which side of a building does it put you on? (Facing it.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ke pīche]{\hi{के} \hi{पीछे} — behind}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-piichhe}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{in front of the station}. Then say the word for a table, which you have had since the chapter on furniture.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{पीछे}}
\textbf{\hi{कुर्सी} \hi{मेज़} \hi{के} \hi{पीछे} \hi{है।}} — The chair is behind the table.

\subsection*{The two words}
Three place words, and they do not all do the same kind of job:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot-three word} & \textbf{what it tells you} \\
\midrule
\hi{पास} & \textbf{how far} — close, no direction \\
\hi{सामने} & \textbf{which side} — facing \\
\hi{पीछे} & \textbf{which side} — away \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\hi{पास}} answers a different question from the other two, and mixing them is the commonest way to get a direction item wrong. A shop can be \textbf{near} a station and still be \textbf{behind} it; it cannot be in front of it and behind it at once.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one glyph worth pausing on}]
\textbf{\hi{पीछे}} carries \textbf{\hi{छ}}, the breathy partner of \textbf{\hi{च}} that the previous chapter taught. This is its first outing in an ordinary word rather than a number, and it is worth saying slowly: the breath belongs to the \textbf{\hi{छ}}, not to the vowel either side of it.

Get that wrong and you say a different word. The pair \textbf{\hi{च} / \hi{छ}} does the same work here that \textbf{\hi{त} / \hi{थ}} does elsewhere, and both pairs punish the same inattention.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{कुर्सी} \hi{मेज़} \hi{के} \hi{पीछे} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{कुर्सी} \hi{मेज़} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of the three place words says nothing about direction
  \item the two facts a listener gets from \textbf{\hi{पीछे}} that \textbf{\hi{पास}} withholds
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{behind the table}? (\textbf{\hi{मेज़} \hi{के} \hi{पीछे}}.) Which place word gives distance without direction? (\textbf{\hi{पास}}.) Which two are opposite ends of one axis? (\textbf{\hi{सामने}} and \textbf{\hi{पीछे}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[parivār ke liye]{\hi{परिवार} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} — for, with a noun in front}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-ke-liye}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{for me} in Hindi — you have had it since the possessive chapter. Then say the word for a family.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{के} \hi{लिए}}
\textbf{\hi{यह} \hi{परिवार} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{है।}} — This is for the family.

\subsection*{The two words}
\textbf{\hi{मेरे} \hi{लिए}} was taught as a phrase to memorise. It was never a phrase. It was this shape with a possessive in slot 1:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot 1} & \textbf{slot 2} & \textbf{slot 3} \\
\midrule
\hi{मेरे} & — & \hi{लिए} \\
\hi{परिवार} & \hi{के} & \hi{लिए} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The top row has no separate slot 2 because \textbf{\hi{मेरे}} already \textbf{is} the possessive, bent. When slot 1 is a noun instead, the possessive has to be supplied, and \textbf{\hi{के}} is what supplies it.

That is the whole difference between the two rows, and it is the same difference that runs through this chapter: a pronoun carries its own \textbf{\hi{के}} inside itself, a noun does not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: what \emph{for} covers}]
\textbf{\hi{के} \hi{लिए}} covers two things English also puts under \emph{for}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sense} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
who benefits & \hi{यह} \hi{परिवार} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{है।} \\
what something is meant to do & \hi{यह} \hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{है।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The second sense is the one the next lesson builds on, because a \textbf{purpose} is usually an action rather than a thing, and an action needs one more change before it can stand in slot 1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यह} \hi{परिवार} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{यह} \hi{मेरे} \hi{लिए} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item why the second one has no \textbf{\hi{के}} in it
  \item the two senses \textbf{\hi{के} \hi{लिए}} carries
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{for the family}? (\textbf{\hi{परिवार} \hi{के} \hi{लिए}}.) Why does \textbf{\hi{मेरे} \hi{लिए}} lack a middle word? (The pronoun is already carrying the possessive.) What is still missing before you can say \emph{for doing} something? (A change to the verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[karne ke liye]{\hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} — in order to}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-karne-ke-liye}



\begin{quote}
Say the infinitive \emph{to do}. Now say \emph{for the family}. To put the first inside the second, one of them has to bend — and by now you can guess which.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए}}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{जाता} \hi{हूँ।}} — I go in order to work.

\textbf{\hi{करना}} became \textbf{\hi{करने}}. Nothing else moved.

\begin{cousinweb}
Look at the ending that changed, and then look at where you have seen that change before:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{kind of word} & \textbf{plain} & \textbf{before a postposition} \\
\midrule
possessive & \hi{मेरा} & \hi{मेरे} \\
demonstrative possessive & \hi{उसका} & \hi{उसके} \\
own & \hi{अपना} & \hi{अपने} \\
noun & \hi{बच्चा} & \hi{बच्चे} \\
\textbf{infinitive} & \textbf{\hi{करना}} & \textbf{\hi{करने}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five kinds of word, one ending, one trigger. The infinitive is the \textbf{last} of the five, and it needs no new rule at all: \textbf{-\hi{ना}} ends in \textbf{-\hi{आ}}, so it bends exactly as \textbf{\hi{बच्चा}} does.

The reason it can bend like a noun is that in Hindi it \textbf{is} one. \textbf{\hi{करना}} is both \emph{to do} and \emph{the doing}, which is why it could already sit where a noun sits. A word that behaves like a noun bends like a noun.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the purpose goes}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot} & \textbf{contents} \\
\midrule
1 & who \\
2 & the purpose: \textbf{\hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए}} \\
3 & the main verb, last \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English puts the purpose \textbf{after} the verb — \emph{I go to work}. Hindi puts it \textbf{before} — because the verb goes last, and that has not changed since the first sentence you read.

So the order reverses, and the reversal is the only thing to practise. The pieces themselves are all old.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{जाता} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \textbf{\hi{करना}} turns into, and what it turns into it for
  \item the five kinds of word that wear this ending
  \item which end of the sentence a Hindi purpose sits at
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{in order to work}? (\textbf{\hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए}}.) What made \textbf{\hi{करना}} bend? (A postposition was coming.) Why can an infinitive bend like a noun? (Because it is one.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sambandh kī tālikā]{sambandh kī tālikā — relation, on one page}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-repaso-sambandh}



\begin{quote}
Name the word for \emph{with} and the word for \emph{in front of}, and say what the two phrases have in the middle.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the six}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot 3} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\hi{साथ} & with & company \\
\hi{बिना} & without & absence \\
\hi{पास} & near & distance \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and the other three}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot 3} & \textbf{English} & \textbf{what it does} \\
\midrule
\hi{सामने} & in front of & facing side \\
\hi{पीछे} & behind & far side \\
\hi{लिए} & for & benefit or purpose \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Six words, and \textbf{not one of them is a new piece of grammar}. Each is a noun sitting in a possessive phrase. \textbf{\hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ}} is \emph{the friend's company} and \textbf{\hi{घर} \hi{के} \hi{पास}} is \emph{the house's nearness}, and Hindi is content to leave it at that.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the one word that never changes}]
Slot 2 is \textbf{\hi{के}} every single time, whatever stands on either side of it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{slot 1} & \textbf{slot 2} & \textbf{slot 3} \\
\midrule
\hi{दोस्त} & \hi{के} & \hi{साथ} \\
\hi{घर} & \hi{के} & \hi{पास} \\
\hi{करने} & \hi{के} & \hi{लिए} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

It is \textbf{\hi{के}} rather than \textbf{\hi{का}} or \textbf{\hi{की}} because there is a further word coming, and a possessive in front of a further word goes oblique. That is the same rule the noun chapter taught and the same rule the possessive chapter taught, applied a third time.

When slot 1 is a pronoun, slot 2 disappears into it: \textbf{\hi{मेरे} \hi{पास}}, \textbf{\hi{मेरे} \hi{लिए}}. The \textbf{\hi{के}} is still there — it is the \textbf{-\hi{ए}} you can hear on \textbf{\hi{मेरे}}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{चाय} \hi{के} \hi{बिना}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मेज़} \hi{के} \hi{पीछे}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one word that sits in slot 2 every time
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many slots does a Hindi relation phrase have? (Three.) Which slot is always the same? (The second.) What happens to that slot when slot 1 is a pronoun? (It fuses into the pronoun's own ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dukān kahā̃ hai?]{\hi{दुकान} \hi{कहाँ} \hi{है}? — answering with a landmark}

\label{lesson:HI-C93-sintesis-sambandh}



\begin{quote}
Ask where the shop is. You have been able to ask this for a long time, and until this chapter you could not answer it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{speaker} & \textbf{Hindi} \\
\midrule
A & \hi{दुकान} \hi{कहाँ} \hi{है}? \\
B & \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} \hi{है।} \\
A & \hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{पास}? \\
B & \hi{हाँ}, \hi{पास} \hi{है।} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

B's first answer gives a \textbf{side}; the second gives only a \textbf{distance}. B is not repeating — B is conceding the weaker claim, because A asked for less.

\subsection*{How to answer}
Find the \textbf{landmark} — the noun before \textbf{\hi{के}} — then read the word after it, because that word alone carries the relation.

\textbf{\hi{पास}} gives distance and no side. \textbf{\hi{सामने}} and \textbf{\hi{पीछे}} give a side and no distance. Do not upgrade \textbf{\hi{पास}} into a side.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the chapter in one sentence}]
Hindi has no prepositions. It has \textbf{possessive phrases whose head noun names a relation}.

\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ} \hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{जाता} \hi{हूँ।}} — Two relation phrases, one sentence, three slots each.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{दुकान} \hi{कहाँ} \hi{है}?\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{स्टेशन} \hi{के} \hi{सामने} \hi{है}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}\hi{मैं} \hi{दोस्त} \hi{के} \hi{साथ} \hi{काम} \hi{करने} \hi{के} \hi{लिए} \hi{जाता} \hi{हूँ}\textquotedblright{}
  \item which of the place words would be a wrong answer to \emph{which side?}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where in a relation phrase does the landmark sit? (Before \textbf{\hi{के}}.) Which word carries the relation? (The one after \textbf{\hi{के}}.) Which relation word tells you nothing about direction? (\textbf{\hi{पास}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
